cards.q: What is the clinical definition of normal labour (eutocia)?
cards.a: Spontaneous expulsion of a **viable, mature singleton fetus** presenting by the **vertex** through the maternal birth canal within **24 hours**, without maternal or fetal trauma, and without surgical intervention beyond an **indicated episiotomy**.

cards.q: What gestational age ranges define abortion, preterm labour, full-term delivery, and post-term gestation?
cards.a:
• Non-viable / Abortion: Termination prior to **28 weeks**.
• Premature (Preterm): Expulsion between **28 and 36 weeks** (or <37 completed weeks).
• Full-Term / Mature: Delivery between **37 and 42 weeks** (canonically **38–40 weeks**).
• Post-mature (Post-term): Gestation exceeding **40 to 42 weeks**.

cards.q: What percentage of normal physiological deliveries present in cephalic vertex presentation, and what are the main malpresentations?
cards.a:
• Vertex presentation: **~95%**
• Breech presentation: **~4%**
• Transverse lie (shoulder) presentation
• Cord presentation/prolapse: **~0.5%** (causes acute fetal asphyxia requiring immediate delivery).

cards.q: What criteria exclude an otherwise uncomplicated delivery from being classified as eutocia regarding assistance and passage?
cards.a: Exclusions include delivery via **Cesarean section**, extrauterine implantations, or requiring instrumental assistance like **obstetric forceps** or **Ventouse vacuum extractor**.

cards.q: What are the common risks and standard management associated with post-mature labour?
cards.a: Risks include **placental senescence** and **oligohydramnios**; management requires **active induction of labour** via **exogenous oxytocin infusions** (or Cesarean delivery if induction fails).

cards.q: What defines prolonged labour temporally, and what are its four primary etiologies?
cards.a:
Defined as active labour cumulative duration **exceeding 24 hours**.
• Etiologies: **Uterine inertia**, **occipitoposterior position**, **rigid perineum (elderly primigravida)**, and **full bladder and rectum**.

cards.q: What are the optimal and malpositioned cephalic occiput positions and their incidence?
cards.a:
• Optimal: **Occiput Anterior (OA)** accounting for **80%** (**60% LOA**, **20% ROA**).
• Malposition: **Occiput Posterior (OP)** accounting for **~20%** (**15% ROP**, **5% LOP**), which causes severe maternal low back pain and protracted descent.

cards.q: Why does a distended bladder or rectum impede labour progress, and how is it managed?
cards.a: They cause spatial encroachment on the mid-pelvic cavity, exerting **mechanical resistance** to fetal descent. Relieved by **evacuation via enema** and **voiding every 2 hours**.

cards.q: What defines precipitate labour, and what maternal and neonatal risks does it carry?
cards.a:
Labour terminating in **less than 3 hours** due to hyperactive contractions against low resistance.
• Maternal risks: **extensive perineal lacerations** and **uterine inversion**.
• Neonatal risks: **intracranial hemorrhage**, **rapid hypoxia**, and **unattended birth trauma**.

cards.q: What is 'the show' and what causes its appearance at the onset of labour?
cards.a: Discharge of the **cervical mucous plug tinged with blood**, caused by **effacement of the lower uterine segment** separating the fetal membranes from decidua and tearing **miniature cervical capillaries**.

cards.q: How do true labour pains differ from false labour pains (Braxton Hicks) regarding cervical changes, palpation, and sedation response?
cards.a:
• True pains: **progressive cervical effacement & dilatation**, uterus becomes **board-like hard**, and **not relieved by sedation**.
• False pains: **no cervical dilatation**, uterus remains **relatively soft**, and **promptly relieved by sedation or rest**.

cards.q: How do true labour pains differ from false labour pains regarding pain radiation and enema response?
cards.a:
• True pains: Radiate from lower abdomen to **lumbosacral region and thighs**, and are **enhanced by enema**.
• False pains: Confined to **lower abdomen/groin (non-radiating)**, and **relieved/unaffected by enema**.

cards.q: What are the primary physiological functions of liquor amnii?
cards.a: Provides **free fetal movement** (prevents amniotic adhesions), acts as a **hydraulic shock absorber**, maintains **thermal regulation**, functions as an **excretory/metabolic reservoir**, and acts as an intrapartum **cervical wedge (forewaters)** for internal os dilatation.

cards.q: What is the biomechanical difference between skeletal muscle relaxation and uterine retraction?
cards.a: Instead of returning to original resting length, myometrial fibers maintain a **semi-relaxation / half-relaxation state**, fixating at a **shorter, thicker baseline** after each contraction cycle.

cards.q: What are the four clinical values of uterine retraction?
cards.a:
1. Assists in **dilatation of the cervix**.
2. Assists in **expulsion of the fetus**.
3. Assists in **separation of the placenta**.
4. Controls **postpartum bleeding** (acting as living ligatures around intramural blood vessels).

cards.q: What constitute the auxiliary forces of labour, and in which stage are they primarily utilized?
cards.a: Voluntary and involuntary contractions of **maternal abdominal wall muscles and diaphragm** ('bearing-down efforts'), generated primarily during the **second stage of labour**.

cards.q: What are the defined boundaries and normal durations of the first stage of labour?
cards.a:
Spans from **true labour onset** until **full cervical dilatation (10 cm / 5 fingers)**.
• Duration: **8 to 12 hours** in primigravidae; **6 to 8 hours** in multiparae.

cards.q: What are the boundaries and standard duration of the second stage of labour?
cards.a: Spans from **complete cervical dilatation (10 cm)** to **complete expulsion of the fetus**, lasting from **a few minutes up to 2 hours**.

cards.q: What are the boundaries, duration, and mechanism of the third stage of labour?
cards.a: Spans from fetal delivery to **complete expulsion of placenta and membranes**, typically lasting **15 to 30 minutes**, mediated by **myometrial retraction shearing the placental site**.

cards.q: What is the fourth stage of labour, and what is the primary clinical priority during this time?
cards.a: The **first 24 hours postpartum**, dedicated to preventing and monitoring for **primary postpartum hemorrhage (uterine atony)** and **ascending infection / puerperal fever**.

cards.q: What are the sequential cardinal movements of the fetal head during normal labour?
cards.a:
1. **Engagement**
2. **Descent**
3. **Flexion**
4. **Internal Rotation**
5. **Extension**
6. **Restitution & External Rotation**

cards.q: What fetal head diameter enters the pelvic inlet during engagement, and what diameter presents upon flexion?
cards.a:
• Engagement: **Biparietal diameter (9.5 cm)**.
• Flexion: Replaces larger diameters with the **suboccipitobregmatic diameter (9.5 cm)**.

cards.q: What anatomical structure mediates internal rotation of the fetal head, and what is its path?
cards.a: The gutter-like slope of the **levator ani (pelvic floor)** directs the occiput anteromedially from an **oblique diameter** into the **anteroposterior diameter** of the pelvic outlet.

cards.q: Why is maternal bearing down strictly contraindicated during the first stage of labour?
cards.a: Bearing down against an incompletely dilated cervix causes **maternal exhaustion**, **cervical edema**, and **cervical tissue tears**.

cards.q: Why is upright ambulation encouraged with intact membranes, but lateral recumbency mandated upon membrane rupture?
cards.a:
• Ambulation uses gravity to promote descent.
• Lateral recumbency post-ROM prevents **umbilical cord prolapse** and excessive loss of liquor amnii.

cards.q: What is the normal fetal heart rate (FHR) range, and what values indicate fetal distress?
cards.a:
• Normal: **110–160 bpm**.
• Distress: **<100 bpm** (bradycardia), **>160 bpm** (tachycardia), or persistent irregular rhythm.

cards.q: What breathing pattern should the mother adopt during bearing-down contractions versus at the moment of crowning?
cards.a:
• Bearing down: **Costal breathing** to maintain intra-abdominal pressure.
• At crowning: **Pant and stop pushing entirely** to allow slow delivery via passive uterine recoil and avoid perineal blowout.

cards.q: Why is gentle fundal massage indicated during the third stage of labour?
cards.a: Stimulates myometrial mechanoreceptors to produce **tonic contraction and rapid retraction**, constricting sheared spiral arterioles to prevent **primary postpartum hemorrhage**.

cards.q: What are the three main functional values of postpartum physical therapy exercises?
cards.a:
1. **Prophylactic**: Prevents DVT, prolapse, incontinence, and diastasis recti.
2. **Curative**: Resolves perineal edema, restores pelvic floor tone, and aids lochial drainage.
3. **Lactational**: Boosts circulation, relieves posture strain, and promotes **prolactin/oxytocin release**.

cards.q: What are the absolute contraindications to initiating postpartum exercises?
cards.a:
• **Postpartum haemorrhage**
• **Nephritis**
• **Puerperal fever**

cards.q: What exercises are prescribed on the first postpartum day, and what is the benefit of prone lying?
cards.a:
• Exercises: Deep breathing, circulatory ankle pumps, static abdominal exercises, and **prone relaxation on face**.
• Prone lying creates **forward uterine displacement**, promoting **uterine involution** and **lochial drainage**.

cards.q: Which exercise is introduced on Day 2 postpartum to treat perineal edema, and what is its mechanism?
cards.a: **Pelvic floor exercises (Kegels)**; voluntary contractions produce a **mechanical pumping action** that accelerates venous and lymphatic drainage of interstitial fluid.

cards.q: What exercises are introduced on Days 3, 4, and 5 of the postpartum exercise protocol?
cards.a:
• Day 3: **Pelvic rocking**.
• Day 4: **Hip shrugging**, **pelvic rotation**, and **posture correction**.
• Day 5: First step of **trunk flexion**.

cards.q: What is the exercise progression for Day 6, Day 7, and Day 8 onward postpartum?
cards.a:
• Day 6: First step of **trunk rotation**.
• Day 7: Progression of other trunk flexion and rotation steps.
• Day 8: Increase repetitions **up to 20 times** daily through the end of the puerperium.

cards.q: What is an episiotomy, when is it performed, and under what anesthesia?
cards.a: A surgical incision into the perineum during the **second stage of labour as the fetal head crowns** (exterior distension **3–4 cm**), performed under **local infiltration anesthesia**.

cards.q: What anatomical structures are damaged in 1st-degree and 2nd-degree perineal tears?
cards.a:
• 1st Degree: **Fourchette, perineal skin, and vaginal mucosa** (no muscle).
• 2nd Degree: Perineal subcutaneous tissue and muscles (**superficial transverse perineal** and **bulbocavernosus**; spares deep transverse perineal).

cards.q: What anatomical structures are damaged in 3rd-degree and 4th-degree perineal tears?
cards.a:
• 3rd Degree: Disruption of the **anal sphincter complex (EAS ± IAS)**.
• 4th Degree: Both external and internal anal sphincters plus the **anorectal epithelium (rectal mucosa)**, exposing the rectal lumen.

cards.q: What are the primary maternal and fetal indications for an episiotomy?
cards.a:
• Maternal: **Elderly primipara (≥35 years)**, **rigid perineum**, **perineal scar**, **vulvar edema**, or **instrumental deliveries (forceps/Ventouse)**.
• Fetal: **Fetal distress**, **malposition/malpresentation**, **fetal macrosomia (≥3.5–4.0 kg)**, and **prematurity**.

cards.q: What are the advantages and the primary disadvantage of a median (midline) episiotomy?
cards.a:
• Advantages: **Easy to repair**, **rare dyspareunia**, **rare faulty healing**, **minimal blood loss**, and **less postoperative pain**.
• Disadvantage: **High risk of extension through the anal sphincter and rectum**.

cards.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of a mediolateral episiotomy?
cards.a:
• Advantage: **Extension into the anal sphincter and rectum is rare**.
• Disadvantages: **Technically difficult to repair**, **higher blood loss**, **more postoperative pain**, and **higher rates of faulty healing and dyspareunia**.

cards.q: What are the acute and chronic complications of an episiotomy?
cards.a:
• Acute: **Pain**, **edema**, **hematoma**, **hemorrhage**, **infection**, and **sphincter tear extension**.
• Chronic: **Persistent dyspareunia**, **pelvic floor dysfunction (incontinence/prolapse)**, and **rectovaginal or anovaginal fistulae**.

cards.q: What are the physical therapy parameters for cryotherapy and pulsed ultrasound in acute episiotomy pain?
cards.a:
• Cryotherapy: **20 minutes**, up to **6 times/day (every 2 hours)**.
• Pulsed Ultrasound: **3 MHz**, **0.5 W/cm²**, **1:1 pulsed ratio**, for **5 minutes/day** via an **indirect water/gel glove technique**.

cards.q: What are the physical therapy parameters for LLLT and TENS in acute episiotomy pain?
cards.a:
• LLLT: Non-contact, **0.5–4 J/cm²**, **15 mW**, maximal pulsing frequency, **90 seconds per region**.
• TENS: Conventional **high (100 Hz)** or low **(5 Hz)** for **30 minutes**, placed parallel/straddling the wound.

cards.q: What are the settings for Pulsed Electromagnetic Energy (PEMF) in acute vs chronic perineal tissue management?
cards.a:
• Acute: Pulse width **40–65 µs**, frequency **10–220 pulses/s**, **20 minutes twice daily**.
• Chronic: Administered to facilitate **organized fibrin realignment** and suppress hypertrophic cross-linked scar tissue.

cards.q: What are the specific laser parameters for wound healing vs scar remodeling in chronic perineal pain?
cards.a:
• Wound Healing: Wavelength **600–750 nm**, frequency **<1000 Hz**, energy density **0.5–2 J/cm²**.
• Scar Remodeling: Wavelength **750–900 nm**, frequency **>1000 Hz**, energy density **4–6 J/cm²**.

cards.q: How is continuous ultrasound utilized in the chronic stage of episiotomy healing?
cards.a: Administered in **continuous (thermal) mode** for **8 sessions** to enhance collagen viscoelasticity, realign irregular fibers, and restore tissue extensibility.

cards.q: How are TENS electrodes placed to relieve pain during the first stage of labour?
cards.a:
• Upper pair: Paravertebral at **T10–L1** (targeting uterine sympathetic innervation).
• Lower pair: Centered over **S2–S4** (targeting referred sacral back pain).

cards.q: What are the specific TENS stimulation parameters used during the first stage of labour?
cards.a:
• Frequency: **80–120 Hz**
• Pulse Width: **150 µs**
• Intensity: Adjusted to patient tolerance until **tingling/numbness** is felt, maintained across the **entire first stage**.

cards.q: How is back effleurage massage executed during the first stage of labour, and when is it most effective?
cards.a: Long, gliding flat-hand strokes moving from the **base of the spine up to the shoulders on inhalation**, then down the sides on exhalation; applied **between contractions** to promote relaxation and **endorphin release**.

cards.q: How is back kneading massage performed during the first stage of labour?
cards.a: Firm, slow, rhythmic finger-squeezing motions applied while sitting astride a chair or leaning forward, directed to the **lower back (between spine and iliac crest)**, upper back, and shoulders.
